Step 26: Hydrate Initial State
↑ top

This step shows how a service can provide asynchronous initial State to a service-owned . Before the service calls initialize(), it registers a deferred hydrate() factory. Initialization then waits for that factory to resolve or reject before the FeatureCell can finish its first State request.

In this example, example.hydrate.ts is only a teaching helper. It creates a Promise, keeps its resolver and rejecter, and exposes those controls to the example component so you can choose when initialization completes. A real hydration factory would use the same boundary to consume a database query, an API response, persisted application data, or another asynchronous source. The helper does not represent that production data-access layer.

The configured initialState still exists, but the deferred hydration result is authoritative for initialization. A successful result continues through the normal Resolve, Filter, Reducer, and Emit pipeline. If the hydration Promise rejects, the initialization request enters Error State instead of falling back to initialState or persistence.

This step does not introduce a new UI workflow or redesign the character editor. The visible teaching interaction is limited to the Resolve and Reject buttons, with the existing state.isLoading() indicator showing that the initial request is waiting. Once you settle the request, the page continues with the same UI so you can focus on the FeatureCell lifecycle.

Take Action
  1. Open example.hydrate.ts and identify the Promise, stored resolver, and stored rejecter used only to hold the tutorial request open.
  2. Open example.service.ts and follow the registration of that helper with hydrate() before initialize().
  3. Open example.component.ts and follow how the Resolve and Reject buttons settle the helper's Promise.
What to Look For
  • hydrate() registers the deferred source without executing it. The factory runs when initialize() begins, while the Fluent API keeps asynchronous initialization and its error handling inside the FeatureCell pipeline.
  • Resolve completes initialization and sends the helper's collection through the configured pipeline.
  • Reject produces initialization Error State without falling back to the configured initial value or persistence.
  • state.isLoading() remains true while the helper's Promise is pending and returns to false after completion.
  • The component supplies the teaching controls; the service and FeatureCell still own initialization and State authority.
  • After reloading the example, the existing loading indicator remains visible until you click Resolve or Reject to complete initialization.

Step 27: Resolve a Promise
↑ top

This step shows how to submit a Promise-backed State update after the FeatureCell has initialized. The service passes a deferred factory to mergeState(), allowing the Promise Resolve stage to await its value before the candidate continues through the rest of the pipeline.

In this example, example.promise.ts is a teaching helper. It creates one pending Promise, stores its resolver and rejecter, and lets the component decide when the simulated request completes. A real Promise factory would consume an asynchronous database, API, or other application service. The helper only makes the pending interval visible so you can observe the FeatureCell lifecycle.

The deferred Promise is not resolved by the component. The component starts the request and exposes the teaching controls, while the service submits the input through mergeState(). The FeatureCell owns loading and error State, and the resolved characters continue through the configured Filter and Reducer stages before the array-append merge commits them to State.

This step does not introduce a new UI workflow. The existing Fetch with Promise, Resolve, and Reject buttons make the Promise lifecycle visible, and the existing state.isLoading() indicator shows while the request is pending. The surrounding character editor remains the same so you can focus on how a Promise enters the FeatureCell pipeline.

Take Action
  1. Open example.promise.ts and identify the pending Promise, stored resolver, and stored rejecter used to hold the tutorial request open.
  2. Open example.service.ts and follow how the deferred Promise is submitted through mergeState().
  3. Open example.component.ts and follow how the Fetch, Resolve, and Reject actions delegate to the helper and service without accessing the FeatureCell directly.
What to Look For
  • Click Fetch with Promise and observe the loading indicator while the helper's Promise remains pending.
  • Click Resolve to complete the Promise and watch its characters enter Filter and Reducer stages before the array-append merge commits them.
  • The deferred factory is consumed once for the pipeline request, so Promise resolution stays associated with that FeatureCell execution.
  • Reload the example, start the request again, and click Reject to see the Promise rejection become normalized pipeline Error State while the previously committed collection is preserved.
  • The component supplies the teaching controls; the service and FeatureCell own loading, error, resolution, and commit behavior.

Step 28: Resolve an Observable
↑ top

This step shows how to submit an Observable-backed State update after the FeatureCell has initialized. The service passes the Observable to mergeState(), allowing the Observable Resolve stage to subscribe to the source and extract its emitted value before the candidate continues through the pipeline.

In this example, example.observable.ts is a teaching helper. It creates a controlled ReplaySubject, exposes it as an Observable, and lets the component decide when the source emits or errors. A real Observable could represent a stream from an API, database, event source, or another application service. The helper only keeps the source pending long enough for you to observe the Resolve lifecycle.

The Observable is not subscribed to by the component. The component starts the request and exposes the teaching controls, while the service submits the source through mergeState(). The FeatureCell owns the subscription lifecycle, loading and error State, and downstream processing. The first emitted collection continues through Filter and Reducer stages before the array-append merge commits it to State.

This step does not introduce a new UI workflow. The existing Add by Observable, Emit, and Error buttons make the source lifecycle visible, and the existing state.isLoading() indicator shows while the Observable is pending. The surrounding character editor remains the same so you can focus on how an Observable enters the FeatureCell pipeline.

Take Action
  1. Open example.observable.ts and identify the controlled Subject, Observable wrapper, emitter, and error callback used to hold the tutorial source open.
  2. Open example.service.ts and follow how the Observable is submitted through mergeState().
  3. Open example.component.ts and follow how the Add, Emit, and Error actions delegate to the helper and service without subscribing in the component.
What to Look For
  • Click Add by Observable and observe the loading indicator while the helper's source remains pending.
  • Click Emit to produce the source value and watch the first emitted collection enter Filter and Reducer stages before the array-append merge commits it.
  • Repeat the request and click Error to see the Observable error normalized into pipeline Error State while the previously committed collection is preserved.
  • The Observable Resolve stage owns subscription and extracts a single emitted value for downstream processing; the component only supplies the teaching controls.
  • state.isLoading() remains active while the Observable is pending and completes with the resolved or error State.

Step 29: Resolve an HTTP Resource
↑ top

This step shows how to submit Angular's HttpResourceRef as a State input after the FeatureCell has initialized. The service creates the resource and passes it to replaceState(), allowing the HTTP Resource Resolve stage to observe its reactive value signal and wait for the first concrete response before the candidate continues through the pipeline.

In this example, example.http-resource.ts is a teaching adapter around the public SWAPI people endpoint. It selects the people needed by the tutorial, converts the untrusted response into the application's character shape, and rejects incomplete data before it reaches State. A real adapter could map an application's own HTTP response, but it would follow the same boundary: create a resource, parse its response, and submit the typed result to the FeatureCell.

The component does not read the HTTP resource directly. It starts the request, while the service submits the resource through replaceState(). The HTTP Resource Resolve stage synchronizes the resource's loading and error signals with the pipeline, then sends the parsed characters through Filter and Reducer stages before the replacement collection is committed atomically to State.

This step does not introduce a new UI workflow. The existing Replace with httpResource button starts the request, and the existing state.isLoading() indicator shows while the resource is pending. The surrounding character editor remains the same so you can focus on how an Angular HTTP resource enters the FeatureCell pipeline.

Take Action
  1. Open example.http-resource.ts and identify the HTTP resource, selected remote records, response parser, and validation errors.
  2. Open example.service.ts and follow how the resource is submitted through replaceState().
  3. Open example.component.ts and follow how the HTTP Resource button delegates to the service without reading the resource or owning its lifecycle.
What to Look For
  • Click Replace with httpResource and observe the existing collection and loading indicator while the HTTP resource is pending.
  • The HTTP Resource Resolve stage observes the resource rather than the component, then extracts the first concrete value for pipeline processing.
  • After the response is parsed and validated, the selected characters enter Filter and Reducer stages before replacing the previous collection atomically.
  • Transport, parsing, validation, and HTTP failures are normalized into the FeatureCell error lifecycle without committing a partial response.
  • state.isLoading() remains active while the resource is pending and completes with either the replacement or the normalized error State.

Step 30: Complete Async Input Tutorial
↑ top

The async input chapter is complete when you can distinguish initialization-time hydration from later asynchronous state updates and can observe the same FeatureCell loading and error lifecycle across all four input styles.

The component owns only presentation state and user actions. The service owns the FeatureCell boundary and submits each asynchronous source through the appropriate state API. Resolve behavior then determines how each input becomes a candidate for the shared Filter, Reducer, and commit pipeline.

Take Action
  1. Compare example.hydrate.ts with the hydration registration in example.service.ts and identify how the deferred source participates in initialization.
  2. Compare example.promise.ts and example.observable.ts with their service methods and identify how each source is submitted through mergeState().
  3. Open example.http-resource.ts and follow how the resource is created, parsed, validated, and submitted through replaceState().
  4. Compare example.component.ts with the four source files and identify which layer owns source creation, teaching controls, resolution, presentation, and committed State.
What to Look For
  • Resolve and reject hydration to see that the deferred result controls initialization rather than the configured initial value.
  • Resolve and reject the Promise and Observable inputs while watching state.isLoading() and Error State.
  • Run the HTTP Resource request and confirm that its parsed result uses the same downstream Filter, Reducer, and commit pipeline.
  • Across all four inputs, the component supplies teaching controls, the service owns the FeatureCell boundary, and the FeatureCell owns resolution, loading, errors, and committed State.
Async Input Summary
  • hydrate() supplies authoritative initial State during initialization.
  • Promise and Observable inputs resolve deferred values for mergeState().
  • HTTP Resource input resolves a reactive Angular resource for replaceState().
  • All four inputs preserve the service-owned boundary and converge on the same pipeline and reactive State APIs.
